thread.title: Weak Performance In China And India Will Cause Apple To Stagnate - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Michael Blair
title: Weak Performance In China And India Will Cause Apple To Stagnate - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple ( AAPL ) CEO Tim Cook says they have a $300 phone in India. About time. Apple has a 2% market share in India which is among the world’s fastest growing smartphone markets. Things are going from bad to worse for Apple in India .
Apple sold about 2.4 million iPhones in India in 2018 according to Counterpoint Research.
According to Counterpoint, one in ten of the world's smartphones is sold in India . Xiaomi ( XI ) and Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) are the market leaders in India, where the market continues to grow at double-digit rates. Apple is an “also-ran.”
Source: IDC
With the global smartphone market declining almost 6% in Q3 2018, India’s double-digit growth is not only a rarity but also an indicator that growth in smartphones is now limited to emerging markets. Lower growth with a greater proportion of sales at lower prices cannot be good for Apple. Fewer iPhone sales implies fewer users buying Apple services in Apple’s “walled garden” and in the low-income emerging markets like India iPhone margins will be slim and services revenue will be scant.
India’s malaise for Apple is small but will become larger over time. A greater problem is that of China where the market is shrinking and Apple is losing share, according to data from Counterpoint.
Source: Counterpoint
Welcome to the world, Apple. Low market share and high prices will take their toll and the future for Apple may be a lot less promising than Tim Cook’s ebullience suggests. Apple investors have lost nearly $400 billion in market value in only a few months. There is little evidence that is going to reverse itself any time soon.
I was several years early in pointing out the longer-term risks of Apple’s strategy which sacrificed market share for short-term margin. That worked well for Apple bulls as the company became the most valuable company on earth amassing massive amounts of cash. That cash will surely be used for share buybacks and dividends and Apple shareholders (who have done very well until recently) will continue to see management prop up earnings through buybacks. Apple’s recent buybacks were above the current market price which I view as destructive rather than helpful to shareholder value.
Warren Buffett was late to the Apple party and now sits on a sizeable loss on his 252 million Apple shares.
Buffett won’t despair. Apple has such a fortress balance sheet the company can pay rising dividends for years to come, but those investors looking for a repeat of the outsized gains they enjoyed on Apple stock for a decade will have to be satisfied with the dividend and little else. The trip from $230 a share to $150 or so has been a short one and the recovery (if there is one) is going to take some time.
Source: Nasdaq
I estimate Apple will earn about $10 a share this year, well below most analysts who forecast earnings per share between $10.51 and $15.40 per share.
If I am right, the share price will continue to move sideways or even fall further.
Apple is a powerhouse with plenty of opportunity to innovate. The company needs a shift in strategy to grow. Services alone limited to Apple’s overpriced devices with the prospect of a shrinking installed base will not do the trick, despite management’s emphasis on services as the next leg of growth. For services to really grow, Apple needs to build its installed base or make services as readily usable by Android and Windows devices as by iOS and OSX.
Building the installed base will require more competitive prices, which Apple has reluctantly recognized in India. Taking down the walls of the “walled garden” is likely anathema to Apple’s culture, despite competitor Microsoft ( MSFT ) recognizing the need for openness and making its flagship software OS agnostic with enormous success. Microsoft now has a market capitalization equal to or greater than that of Apple.
I would avoid Apple stock until management gives clear disclosure of its path to future growth. It is hard to see where that might come from.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours. it (other than from Seeking Alpha).
